references.text: Moses goes out from Pharaoh and cries to the Lord, a pattern that is repeated in connection with the plagues
Moses says he will stretch out his hands toward the Lord, and the thunder and hail will stop - this is the fulfillment of that promise
Moses goes out from Pharaoh and prays to the Lord, who stops the locust plague - the same pattern as here
Solomon prays with outstretched hands toward heaven in the temple, the same prayer posture Moses used
Stretching out hands in prayer is mentioned as a common prayer posture in Israel
The psalmist prays with hands stretched out toward God, the same prayer posture Moses used
Stretching out hands in prayer is a known practice in Israel that the prophet refers to
The description of the thunder, hail, and fire that began - this verse shows that they stopped
This reference shows the repeated pattern in the plague accounts where Moses' prayer is the decisive factor for God's judgment to cease.
Confirms the consistent theological pattern where Moses' prayer outside the city walls is the condition for God's judgment over Egypt to stop.
A thematic parallel showing how Moses' outstretched hand serves as an instrument for both God's judgment on enemies and His deliverance of His people.
Illustrates the repeated pattern in the plague accounts where Moses' prayer is the direct cause of the plagues stopping.
A complementary verse showing the start of the same event (the hail), and together with the source verse, it completes the picture of God as both sending and removing judgment.
A theological contrast where the same action (outstretched hand over water/sky) leads to both judgment and deliverance, demonstrating God's sovereignty over nature.
A thematic parallel showing continuity in Moses' role as intercessor, where his prayer always leads to the cessation of God's punitive judgment.
